Article Title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max get Variable Aperture as 'most important' camera feature: What it means for users
Article Text:
Apple iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max

Aperture is the part of a camera most phone users never see

The useful bit is what happens when you take control

It is not just about low light

The aperture is only on one camera

Apple is adding more control to video too

The idea isn't new to smartphones

The bigger camera change is the combination

What variable aperture actually changes for iPhone users

Apple has added variable aperture to the main camera on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This will offer users a physical way to control how much light reaches the sensor for the first time on an iPhone.The feature sits alongside a new 48MP Fusion Main camera, a redesigned sensor and new Pro Controls. Apple says the six laser-cut blades inside the lens can move between four aperture settings, while the camera can also adjust the aperture automatically depending on the scene.That sounds like a minor hardware upgrade. But it is not. The lens opening affects exposure, depth of field, and how motion is captured, so giving the iPhone aperture control adds something software alone can't quite duplicate.Apple's description is straightforward: "iPhone 18 Pro has a new 48 megapixel fusion main camera with variable aperture for creative control that wasn't possible before," Apple said. "This is the most advanced camera we've ever made."Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. It is measured using f-numbers such as f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0.The lower the f-number, the wider the opening and the more light reaches the sensor.A wider aperture can therefore help in darker conditions. A narrower aperture lets in less light, but it also keeps more of the scene in focus.Most smartphone cameras use a fixed aperture. The lens has one opening, and the phone relies heavily on shutter speed, ISO, and computational photography to handle different lighting conditions.The iPhone 18 Pro changes that for its main camera. Its lens can open as wide as f/1.48 and then stop down to f/1.8, f/2.8 or f/4.0. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size.Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.The camera can make that decision automatically. In a darker scene, it can open the aperture to f/1.48 and let in more light. In brighter conditions, it can narrow the opening.For most people, the automatic system will do most of the work. The Camera app can choose an aperture based on the scene, just as it already decides on exposure and other settings.The difference is that iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max owners can also take control themselves.Apple's new Pro Controls let users manually change aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. A histogram can also be displayed to help judge exposure across a scene.That gives photographers another way to decide how a picture should look, instead of leaving every exposure decision to the camera.The most obvious example is depth of field. At a wider aperture such as f/1.48, the camera can produce more optical background blur when the subject is relatively close and the background is farther away.Stopping down to f/4.0 has the opposite effect. More of the scene can stay in focus, which can help with landscapes or group photos where people stand at different distances from the camera.That matters because a group shot can otherwise leave one person sharp while another, standing slightly farther away, falls outside the plane of focus. A narrower aperture gives the camera more room to keep those subjects in focus.It also gives photographers another option when deliberately introducing motion into an image. A narrower aperture reduces the amount of light entering the lens, making it easier to use a slower shutter speed when conditions are bright enough.The obvious benefit of opening the aperture is light. Apple says the main camera can open to ƒ/1.48 for low-light photography, letting more light reach the sensor.That can give the camera more flexibility before it has to compensate by increasing ISO or slowing the shutter speed. In practical terms, that can help preserve detail and reduce noise, while a fast enough shutter can keep moving subjects sharp.But variable aperture is useful in the opposite direction too.In bright daylight, photographers sometimes want a slower shutter speed to create motion blur. That can be useful with moving water, people, or cars, and it also matters in video, where shutter speed is normally tied to frame rate.A fixed wide aperture can make that difficult in strong sunlight because too much light reaches the sensor even when the shutter is already operating at its fastest useful setting. Stopping the lens down gives the camera another way to reduce exposure.There are limits, though. A range ending at f/4.0 does not eliminate the need for neutral-density filters in every bright-light situation. Photographers who want long exposures in direct sunlight may still need an ND filter to cut the light further.Apple's implementation has an important limitation. The variable aperture is on the main 24mm camera. It does not extend across the entire rear camera system.The ultra-wide and telephoto cameras don't have the same variable-aperture mechanism. That means the new optical control is available only when shooting through the main lens.This is also why the feature should not be viewed as a replacement for the other cameras or for computational photography. Exposure, autofocus, HDR, noise reduction and image processing still determine much of the final photograph.The hardware simply gives the camera another physical variable to work with before those processes take over.Aperture changes also feed into Apple's video features. The new Pro Controls work with video as well as photography, letting users manually adjust settings including aperture and shutter speed. That is especially relevant for people who want more predictable exposure rather than letting the phone change settings during recording.Apple has also added the ability to apply Cinematic effects after capture to videos recorded at up to 60 frames per second. That means users can make this adjustment after recording instead of committing to the effect while shooting.Time-lapse recording now supports 4K and Dolby Vision HDR, while Audio Mix has new algorithms designed to improve voice quality and isolate music.The combination is notable because Apple isn't presenting the variable aperture as an isolated camera specification. It is part of a broader attempt to give users more control over how photos and video are captured and processed.Apple is not the first phone maker to put a variable aperture in a smartphone. Samsung introduced a dual-aperture system with the Galaxy S9 series in 2018. That system switched between f/1.5 and f/2.4 depending on the lighting conditions.Huawei later introduced more flexible variable-aperture systems, while Xiaomi and Honor have also used the technology in flagship phones.The reason it has remained relatively uncommon is fairly simple: fitting a mechanical aperture mechanism into a smartphone camera adds complexity to an already tightly packed module.For years, phone makers instead concentrated on larger sensors, multiple cameras and computational photography. Those technologies can compensate for many of the limitations of a fixed aperture without adding moving parts to the lens.The iPhone 18 Pro's approach is therefore less about replacing computational photography than adding an optical control alongside it.The variable aperture gets most of the attention, but Apple has made several other changes to the camera system.The 48MP Fusion Main camera uses a new sensor and a new computational imaging pipeline that Apple says produces sharper, more detailed images. Photographic Styles now include additional texture and grain controls, giving users more ways to change the look of their photos.Apple has also added persistent subject tracking for photos and video, letting the camera keep following a person even if they temporarily disappear behind someone else in a crowd.Another feature aimed at photographers is Apple Reference Image. When Reference mode is used, the camera captures signed sensor data that Private Cloud Compute turns into what Apple describes as an "unalterable reference image." You can then view the reference alongside the main photograph in the Photos app.The idea is to compare the original sensor-derived reference with the photograph and identify whether changes have been made. Apple says the feature is intended to address image authenticity, particularly for photographers and photojournalists.Apple is also adding metadata support and upcoming support for the SynthID standard to help identify images generated or edited with AI.For someone who simply opens the Camera app and takes pictures, it may not change much. The phone can choose the aperture automatically, just as it already handles most exposure decisions. For people who shoot deliberately, the change is more useful.A wider f/1.48 setting can help in darker scenes. Stopping down can keep more of a group or landscape in focus. Manual aperture control can also be combined with shutter-speed control to create particular motion effects.It can even produce optical effects that fixed-aperture smartphone cameras cannot reproduce in the same way, including changes in how bright points of light appear at narrower apertures.But four aperture settings don't turn the iPhone into a dedicated interchangeable-lens camera. The sensor remains small compared with most conventional cameras, and the amount of natural optical background blur depends heavily on the distance between the camera, subject, and background.For many portraits, Apple's computational Portrait mode will still produce a stronger and more controllable background-blur effect.The same is true for long exposures in bright daylight. The f/1.48-to-f/4.0 range gives photographers more room, but it does not remove the physical limits imposed by available light.That is probably the right way to look at the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture. It gives the camera one more physical control over exposure and focus, while the sensor and software continue to determine what ultimately reaches the screen.For casual users, most of that will happen automatically. For photographers and videographers who want to decide how the shot is captured, the four aperture settings and Pro Controls make the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max considerably more flexible than a fixed-aperture iPhone.
Article Summary: Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size. Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.

Article Title: Google unveils five new sustainability initiatives in India
Article Text: Google is expanding its Solar API to cover more than 300 million rooftops in India, enabling faster and more accurate rooftop solar assessments. Installers can now evaluate a home’s solar potential without an on‑site visit, reducing time and cost. Platforms like Solar Ladder and OpenSolar have already integrated Solar API insights to streamline proposal creation and automate manual roof surveys.Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. The company will receive environmental attributes from the clean electricity generated, helping address electricity‑related emissions across its value chain. This marks Google’s second Scope 3‑focused solar project in India, bringing total added capacity to 300 MW.Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), a climate‑smart farming method that reduces methane emissions and conserves water. The initiative is expected to generate up to 3 million tonnes of CO₂e in near‑term warming impact (GWP20) and conserve billions of gallons of water.NASA‑enabled satellite verification will support monitoring and farmer adoption.The Google Center for Climate Technology has selected three inaugural projects focused on green workforce training and low‑carbon construction materials. Google is adding two new focus areas—water stewardship and waste & circularity—and is inviting proposals via the Manthan Platform. Selected applicants will receive support to develop scalable, data‑driven environmental solutions.Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet, featuring four Indian startups: Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests, and Climitra Carbon. These companies use AI, Geo‑AI, drones and satellite models to empower farmers, scale agroforestry, restore biodiversity, and convert biomass into biochar.These five initiatives reflect Google’s push to combine AI, research partnerships and local innovation to advance sustainable development and climate resilience across India.
Article Summary: Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt a climate‑smart farming method. Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet.

Article Title: 1980s AI Photo trend: 5 ChatGPT prompts to create Kerala-style retro images
Article Text:
ChatGPT '80s photo trend: What makes the images look retro

Here are five ChatGPT prompts to create 1980s Kerala-style AI photos

1. 1980s Kerala family portrait prompt

Prompt: Recreate this photograph as an authentic Malayali family portrait from Kerala in the mid-1980s. Keep everyone's natural facial features, identities and expressions recognisable. Dress the women in traditional Kerala kasavu sarees and the men in period-appropriate shirts and mundus.

Add authentic 1980s hairstyles and simple traditional jewellery. Set the photograph inside a modest Kerala home with wooden furniture and subtle traditional decor.

2. 1980s Kerala wedding portrait prompt

Prompt: Transform this photograph into an authentic Kerala wedding portrait from the 1980s. Retain the original facial features and identities. Dress the woman in a traditional kasavu saree with classic Kerala gold jewellery, and the man in a traditional mundu.

Add natural 1980s hairstyles and a simple wedding-studio backdrop. Use warm studio lighting, soft focus, subtle analogue film grain and slightly faded but realistic colours.

Avoid excessive sepia or artificial ageing.

3. Vintage Malayali woman portrait prompt

Prompt: Recreate this photograph as an authentic 1980s Kerala studio portrait of a Malayali woman. Preserve natural facial features and identity. Add a traditional Kerala saree, classic gold earrings, bangles and a simple bindi, with voluminous 1980s hairstyle inspired by the era.

4. 1980s Kerala college portrait prompt

Prompt: Turn this photograph into an authentic 1980s Kerala college-era portrait. Keep the original face, facial structure and expression recognisable. Add period-appropriate 1980s Indian clothing and hairstyle, with a simple Malayali look. Keep the result photorealistic. Avoid excessive vintage effects, sepia tones or artificial-looking ageing. The photograph should look naturally shot on an analogue camera in the 1980s.

5. Malayalam cinema-inspired portrait prompt

Prompt: Recreate this photograph as an authentic 1980s Malayalam cinema-inspired studio portrait. Keep original facial features, identity and natural expression recognisable. Give me period-accurate 1980s hair, makeup and clothing, with dramatic studio lighting, soft focus, subtle film grain and the look of an analogue camera.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Meet Kelly Liu: The 16-year-old San Jose student who used AI to map dirty air, put pollution sensors in underserved schools and helped push a countywide policy change
Article Text:
Kelly LiuPhoto credit: www.actionfornature.org

Seeing what broad data misses

Using AI to map pollution

Bringing sensors to underserved schools

From evidence to advocacy

Why school air matters

A model for youth-led environmental science

The challenges ahead

A cleaner future begins with visibility

When Kelly Liu looked at air pollution data around San Jose, she noticed something important was missing. Official monitoring stations could show broad regional trends, but they did not always reveal what students were breathing beside busy roads, industrial areas or older school buildings. The 16-year-old student decided to fill that gap by combining artificial intelligence, low-cost pollution sensors and community organising. Her work mapped local air quality, brought monitoring devices to underserved schools and helped build pressure for stronger countywide action. As described by Action for Nature and reported by Hoodline, Kelly’s project grew from a technical experiment into a public campaign, showing how student-led research can make environmental inequality visible and influence policy. Her story is not just about measuring dirty air. It is about giving communities evidence they can use to demand healthier places to learn.Air pollution rarely affects every neighbourhood in the same way. Two schools only a few miles apart may face very different conditions depending on their proximity to highways, warehouses, factories, construction sites or heavily travelled roads.Weather, traffic patterns and building ventilation can also influence the air students breathe during the school day.Traditional monitoring networks are valuable, but their stations are expensive and widely spaced. One monitor may represent conditions across a large area without capturing pollution hotspots near a particular campus. For families and teachers, that can create a frustrating gap between official regional data and their everyday experience.Kelly became interested in that gap while studying air quality in the South Bay. She wanted to understand where pollution was concentrated and whether some schools were receiving less protection than others. Rather than treating available data as complete, she asked what it left out.Kelly used artificial intelligence as a tool for analysing and visualising complex environmental information. By combining available air quality records with location data, traffic patterns and other geographic indicators, she developed maps that could show likely pollution burdens at a more local level.The purpose of AI was not to replace scientific monitoring. It was to help identify patterns, compare communities and direct attention toward places that might deserve closer investigation. Algorithms can process large amounts of information much faster than a person working manually, making it easier to examine relationships between pollution, roadways, school locations and neighbourhood characteristics.The resulting maps helped turn an abstract issue into something people could see. Instead of discussing air quality only through countywide averages, Kelly could show how exposure might vary from one school to another. That visual clarity made the issue more accessible to students, parents, school administrators and policymakers.Still, maps based on models and existing records have limitations. They can suggest where pollution may be high, but sensors are needed to confirm conditions on the ground. Kelly’s work therefore moved beyond digital analysis and into direct community monitoring.Kelly helped place pollution sensors at schools in communities that are often underrepresented in environmental data. These devices can measure factors such as particulate matter, which includes tiny airborne particles capable of entering the lungs. Depending on the equipment, sensors may also track other pollutants or environmental conditions that affect indoor and outdoor air quality.Installing monitors at schools provides a more detailed picture of what students encounter. It can reveal changes during morning drop off, afternoon traffic, nearby construction or wildfire smoke events. It can also help schools understand whether filtration, ventilation and building maintenance are reducing exposure indoors.The focus on underserved schools was central to Kelly’s approach. Environmental monitoring is not only a technical challenge. It is also a question of fairness. Communities with fewer resources may face greater exposure to pollution while having less access to data, medical guidance or political influence. Placing sensors in those schools helped address both problems by producing evidence and involving the people most affected.Students could see readings from their own campuses and connect the information to lessons in science, technology and health. That made air quality a local and tangible subject rather than a distant environmental issue.Collecting data was only one part of Kelly’s work. She also helped communicate the findings and encourage action. Students, parents and community supporters used the information to argue that schools should have stronger air quality protections, including better filtration, monitoring and policies for days when outdoor pollution becomes dangerous.Student advocacy can be especially powerful because it connects policy decisions to the people who spend much of their day inside school buildings. Kelly and other young organisers were not presenting pollution as an abstract statistic. They were asking why some children should learn in environments with higher exposure and fewer safeguards.Their efforts helped push the conversation beyond individual school campuses toward countywide policy. A countywide approach can create consistent standards, reduce disparities between districts and make it easier to secure funding for monitoring and clean air equipment. It also recognises that pollution does not stop at school boundaries.Children are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs and bodies are still developing. They also breathe more air relative to their body size than adults and may spend many hours each day at school. Exposure to fine particles and other pollutants can aggravate asthma, contribute to respiratory problems and affect attendance and concentration.Schools have a practical role in reducing risk. High quality filtration, properly maintained ventilation systems, closed windows during severe pollution events and clear response plans can all help protect students. Outdoor activity policies may also need to account for air quality, especially during wildfire smoke or periods of heavy traffic pollution.Without monitoring, schools may not know when conditions are changing or whether their mitigation efforts are working. Kelly’s project brought attention to that need and showed how comparatively affordable sensors can complement official monitoring networks.Kelly’s work combines research, technology and public engagement in a way that is increasingly important for environmental problem solving. Young people are often portrayed as passive recipients of climate and pollution policy, but Kelly’s project shows them acting as investigators and advocates.Her approach also demonstrates that environmental science does not end with data collection. A map becomes more useful when people can understand it. A sensor becomes more valuable when its results guide a decision. A policy becomes stronger when it responds to evidence gathered from the communities it affects.Action for Nature’s Eco-Hero recognition highlights this combination of initiative and impact. Kelly did not simply build a technical project for a competition. She used technology to investigate an inequality, worked with communities facing exposure and helped move the discussion toward institutional change.Countywide policy changes can provide a foundation, but implementation requires funding, staff and accountability. Sensors must be calibrated and maintained. Data must be interpreted carefully, particularly when low-cost devices are used. Schools need resources to upgrade filters, repair ventilation systems and respond to changing conditions.There is also a need to communicate results without creating unnecessary alarm. Pollution readings can fluctuate, and one measurement does not always establish a long term health risk. Schools and families need clear guidance explaining what the data mean and what actions are appropriate.Kelly’s work points toward a more transparent system in which schools regularly measure air quality, publish understandable information and prioritise improvements where exposure and vulnerability are greatest. That process would make environmental protection more responsive and equitable.Kelly Liu’s story begins with a simple observation: people cannot solve a problem they cannot see. By using AI to map pollution, sensors to gather local evidence and advocacy to bring the findings into policy discussions, she helped make school air quality visible.Her work also offers a practical lesson for other communities. Environmental change does not always start with a major institution or an expensive research programme. It can begin with a student asking better questions, gathering evidence and inviting others to act.For Kelly, the goal is not merely to produce impressive maps or install more monitors. It is to help ensure every student, regardless of neighbourhood or school budget, has the chance to learn in clean and healthy air. That ambition has already taken her project from a San Jose classroom to a broader countywide conversation.
Article Summary: Air pollution rarely affects every neighbourhood in the same way. Two schools only a few miles apart may face very different conditions depending on their proximity to highways, warehouses, factories, construction sites or heavily travelled roads. Traditional monitoring networks are valuable, but their stations are expensive and widely spaced. One monitor may represent conditions across a large area without capturing pollution hotspots.

Article Title: China planted three types of forests on the Loess Plateau; 18 years later, natural forests held 8% more soil moisture
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Natural forests held 8% more soil moisture

How did natural forests improve soil water storage

Image AI generated

Why did natural forests retain more soil moisture

China’s long-running effort to restore the degraded Loess Plateau has revealed a difference between forests planted by people and those allowed to regenerate naturally. Researchers spent 18 years monitoring four forest types in the region, comparing plantations of Pinus tabuliformis, Platycladus orientalis and Robinia pseudoacacia with a natural secondary forest. The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests, while recording greater macroporosity and stronger water movement through the soil. Its soil held more water after rainfall, with average soil water storage reaching around 6 mm, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. Over the 2006–2024 monitoring period, the natural forest consistently maintained higher soil water content, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining moisture trends. The researchers also found that natural forest soils had lower bulk density and higher levels of soil organic carbon and total nitrogen.These differences suggest that allowing forests to recover naturally may improve the soil’s ability to absorb and retain rainfall. The findings could help guide restoration across water-limited landscapes, where choosing suitable forest types is important for balancing vegetation recovery with available water resources.According to the study published in Water Resources Research, titled ‘Natural Forests Accelerate Soil Hydrological Processes and Enhance Water-Holding Capacities Compared to Planted Forests After Long-Term Restoration ’, natural secondary forests had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests. They also had 68.7% greater macroporosity, a 13.7% larger mean equivalent pore diameter and 34.2% higher saturated hydraulic conductivity. The researchers also recorded higher soil organic carbon, field capacity and available water content in the natural forests.The difference was also visible across the 18-year monitoring period. Natural secondary forests consistently maintained higher soil water content, with peak values reaching 0.28 cm³ per cm³, particularly after substantial rainfall. Pinus tabuliformis showed a slight increase in soil moisture over the period, reaching 0.24 cm³ per cm³, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining soil moisture trends, with average values between 0.15 and 0.22 cm³ per cm³.The researchers found clear differences in soil structure between the forests. Natural secondary forest soils had the highest macroporosity and better-connected pores. Their mean macroporosity was 0.113 mm³ per mm³, compared with 0.089 for Robinia pseudoacacia, 0.065 for Platycladus orientalis and 0.047 for Pinus tabuliformis.The natural forests also showed faster soil-water processes during rainfall. Average soil water storage was around 6 mm in the secondary forests, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. The researchers linked this greater storage to the natural forests’ higher macroporosity and pore connectivity, which allowed rainfall to be redistributed and infiltrate the soil more efficiently.Soil moisture in Pinus tabuliformis and Robinia pseudoacacia dropped substantially during the driest period from June to August. In the upper 60 cm of soil, moisture fell. Platycladus orientalis retained more water in deeper layers, but moisture still declined in the upper soil. The secondary forest maintained higher and more stable moisture, particularly in the upper 60 cm.The researchers also found that the secondary forest had lower bulk density, at about 1.0 g per cm³, in the three planted forests. Its soils also contained generally higher levels of total nitrogen and soil organic carbon. The study’s analysis identified soil properties such as bulk density and organic carbon, together with understory plant diversity, as important factors associated with soil hydrological processes and water-holding capacity.

The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests.

Article Title: In 2015, UNICEF turned shipping containers into heated bathrooms for Mongolia’s nomadic schools; 15 movable WASH Houses gave warm water and toilets to 1,400 students

Warm water became part of school life

Representative image of the inside of a heated portable washroom providing warm water, sinks, and toilets for students in a cold rural school community. Image credit: ChatGPT.

A shipping container becomes school infrastructure

For children in Mongolia’s remote herding communities, using a toilet could mean leaving a heated classroom and stepping outside into temperatures far below freezing. Many rural schools and kindergartens depended on outdoor latrines, while access to warm water for washing was limited. The problem was especially difficult in a country where nomadic families move with their livestock and frozen ground can complicate conventional construction.According to UNICEF , the organisation developed relocatable WASH Houses in Mongolia by adapting the principles of insulated shipping-container construction. The units provided toilets and basins with warm running water in heated, well-lit structures that could be connected to classrooms or ger kindergartens. By 2015, 15 WASH Houses had been installed alongside ger kindergartens and regular classrooms, directly benefiting about 1,400 students.The WASH House was developed as a prefabricated and relocatable solution for Mongolia's harsh climate. The organisation worked with local partners to develop several models based on insulated shipping-container structures.Rather than building every facility from scratch at the school site, the units could be manufactured elsewhere and transported to remote communities. The design addressed one of the biggest problems facing sanitation infrastructure in Mongolia: freezing temperatures. The units were insulated and heated, while their water and sanitation systems were designed to operate in winter conditions. They contained toilets and washing facilities supplied with warm water, giving children access to basic hygiene without having to leave the building for an outdoor latrine.The facility’s portability was especially useful for ger schools and kindergartens. A ger is a round tent-like home traditionally used by Mongolian herding families, and schools in remote areas often have to adapt to that way of life. A portable sanitation facility can offer more flexibility compared to a regular building made of bricks and concrete. UNICEF said the units could be adapted to different water and sanitation setups depending on the site. Some could use wells and septic tanks, while others could connect to existing systems.It was not just about making toilets available to them. Water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities affect whether students can access washrooms, maintain personal hygiene, and use toilets safely during the day. UNICEF research on WASH and menstrual health also noted that rural students in Mongolia faced special challenges because sanitation facilities were inadequate and water and separate washing rooms were limited.Research published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health also examined hygiene conditions among Mongolian schoolchildren. A survey of 1,507 fifth-grade pupils in Ulaanbaatar found that access to water and soap at school handwashing facilities was far from universal, showing how infrastructure availability can shape everyday hygiene practices. For the children using the new WASH Houses, the difference was tangible. UNICEF described facilities that allowed pupils to wash with warm water and use toilets inside a heated structure instead of relying on exposed outdoor facilities. The organisation reported that the teachers linked the better WASH conditions with the lack of health-related issues and absenteeism, but this information was not a part of the scientifically controlled evaluation of the WASH Houses. These units solved multiple problems by improving sanitation, reducing children’s exposure to extreme winter weather, and making handwashing easier.The project reflected a broader trend toward designing infrastructure for places where conventional construction is costly or impractical. Mongolia has a short construction season, harsh winters, and long distances between settlements. As a result, it can be difficult to transport materials and build facilities in remote locations. A prefabricated container offered another option, since much of the work could be completed before delivery and the facility could then be connected to local water and sanitation services.The approach did not aim to turn shipping containers into an alternative to regular schools but rather showed that the infrastructure could be adapted to suit the location. An insulated, heated, and mobile bathroom could be built where it was needed without erecting a whole new permanent structure. In remote Mongolian schools, it became a way to provide toilets, hot water, and basic hygiene facilities for children who previously had to endure harsh conditions to meet basic needs.
Article Summary: The WASH House was developed as a prefabricated and relocatable solution for Mongolia's harsh climate. The units were insulated and heated, while their water and sanitation systems were designed to operate in winter conditions. They contained toilets and washing facilities supplied with warm water, giving children access to basic hygiene.

Article Title: In 1948, Oregon buried geothermal pipes beneath a steep section of US 97 to melt three inches of snow an hour; the system operated for nearly 50 years before its iron pipes corroded
Article Text:
Representative image of a snow-covered mountain highway using underground geothermal heat to melt ice and snow. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

Turning underground heat into a snow-free road

In 1948, Klamath Falls, Oregon, became a pioneer in geothermal pavement heating by harnessing underground warmth to manage snow on steep roads. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Nearly five decades beneath the pavement

In the winter of 1948, a steep stretch of road in Klamath Falls, Oregon, became a test site for geothermal energy. Instead of relying on ploughs, salt or other conventional methods, engineers embedded a network of metal pipes beneath the pavement and used underground heat to warm the road. According to the Geo-Heat Centre Quarterly Bulletin , when US 97 was rerouted through downtown Klamath Falls in 1948, the new road included an adverse 8% grade approaching a traffic signal, where winter conditions created traction problems for vehicles. The Oregon Highway Department incorporated a geothermal pavement de-icing experiment into the project. A 419-foot geothermal well transferred heat through a downhole heat exchanger to a 50:50 mixture of ethylene glycol and water, which circulated through a grid of ¾-inch iron pipes installed three inches below the concrete surface and spaced 18 inches apart.Geothermal water was not piped directly beneath the road surface. Instead, the well supplied a downhole heat exchanger, which transferred heat to a closed-loop system containing a glycol-water mixture. The same circulation fluid could then move continuously through the pavement heating system. The Geo-Heat Centre Quarterly Bulletin reported that the system was initially estimated to provide about 350,000 Btu per hour at a flow rate of 20 gallons per minute.At a flow rate of 50 gallons per minute, the reported heat output was about 900,000 Btu per hour. The system was designed to keep the pavement clear of snow at temperatures as low as -10°F, including during snowfall rates of up to three inches per hour.The experiment was significant because it showed a principle central to hydronic pavement heating: heat can be transferred through pipes buried inside a road or bridge deck to warm the surface from below. A later paper in Advances in Civil Engineering described the Klamath Falls installation as the first hydronic pavement heating system using geothermal energy and noted that the approach helped establish a technology that has since been studied with geothermal, solar and other heat sources. For Klamath Falls, however, keeping the system working was more complicated than simply tapping underground warmth. The geothermal well’s output declined over time. Water temperatures at the well declined, reducing the amount of heat available to the system. In the early 1990s, engineers modified the well by extending the downhole heat exchanger so it could reach hotter water at greater depth. The changes allowed the system to keep supplying heat to the pavement without relying on the original setup.Ultimately, the most problematic issue emerged in relation to the pipes. In less than 50 years, corrosion of the original iron grid caused leaks, and by 1997 the system had failed. The failure did not end the use of geothermal energy for snow melting in Klamath Falls. Instead, the system was reconstructed in 1998, with the original iron grid replaced by a network of PEX piping, or cross-linked polyethene, better suited to the demands of the site.The reconstruction project cost approximately $115,000, according to the Geo-Heat Centre Quarterly Bulletin, and the redesigned system covered about 22,000 square feet of road and bridge deck. It was built to provide enough heat to keep the surface clear of snow at temperatures as low as -10°F. What began as an attempt to make a steep Oregon road safer for vehicles ultimately became a long-running demonstration of how geothermal energy could be adapted for winter road maintenance, with the experiment continuing to shape the way engineers approached snow and ice control.
Article Summary: In 1948, Klamath Falls, Oregon, became a pioneer in geothermal pavement heating by harnessing underground warmth to manage snow on steep roads. Engineers embedded a network of metal pipes beneath the pavement and used underground heat to warm the road. The system was designed to keep the pavement clear of snow at temperatures as low as -10°F, including during snowfall rates of up to three inches per hour.

Article Title: In the 1970s, Washington tied thousands of discarded tyres together across 20 Puget Sound reefs to improve bottom fishing; decades later, the ropes failed and more than 100,000 tyres remained underwat
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: Discarded vehicle tyres rest on the seafloor of Puget Sound, where they were once used to create artificial reefs for recreational fishing | ChatGPT

AI REPRESENTATION: Discarded vehicle tyres rest on the seafloor of Puget Sound, where they were once used to create artificial reefs for recreational fishing | ChatGPT

The reefs were built for bottom fishing

A reef material became a cleanup problem

A harbor seal along the coast of the Puget Sound | Wikimedia Commons

More than 100,000 tires are still being dealt with

Washington's experiment with artificial reefs in Puget Sound began with the practical goal of creating more structure on the seafloor for rockfish, lingcod and other bottom-dwelling fish while expanding recreational fishing opportunities. Discarded vehicle tires, among other materials, were bundled together and lowered into the water at 20 reef sites during the 1970s.A 2025 article from the University of Washington's School of Marine and Environmental Affairs describes the tire reefs as one of Puget Sound's clearest examples of how artificial habitat can produce unintended problems. The tires were tied together with polypropylene rope, and thousands were placed at each of the 20 sites.The University of Washington account says new federal laws and court decisions in the 1970s and 1980s tightened restrictions on salmon fishing, which prompted recreational anglers to put more attention on bottom fishing for species such as rockfish and lingcod. Washington's Department of Fish and Wildlife worked with recreational fishing groups as artificial reef construction expanded. Tires were only one of several materials used, while other reefs incorporated concrete, natural rock, plastics, PVC, vessels, barges and even train cars.The basic idea was to add vertical relief and structural complexity to parts of the seabed that provided relatively little cover.Natural rocky reefs provide crevices and surfaces where algae and invertebrates can live, while smaller fish can use the structure for shelter from predators and currents. The polypropylene rope deteriorated, which allowed individual tires and sections of the artificial structures to move away from their original locations. The tires became loose objects on the seafloor and, in some locations, eventually reached shorelines, instead of remaining as stable reef units. The Washington Department of Natural Resources now considers the old tire structures an environmental problem rather than a successful fish habitat, and its Tire Pile Removal Program says thousands of surplus automotive tires were placed on the bottom of Puget Sound during the 1970s and 1980s to attract native reef fish and improve recreational fishing. The agency says the artificial structures have since been judged unsuccessful and has begun planning and carrying out their removal.DNR began prioritizing removal work in 2019 and has worked with the Washington Department of Ecology, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission and Washington Scuba Alliance to locate and survey the old reefs. DNR's survey work between 2019 and 2021 examined 20 locations using multibeam sonar and underwater video. Tires were found at 14 of those sites, with major differences between locations in the number of tires and the size of the affected areas.The University of Washington report says that the material has weathered and fragmented, while chemical compounds associated with degraded tires can enter the surrounding environment. It also notes that tire surfaces did not provide the same biological communities found on more suitable artificial reef materials.A March 2025 KING 5 report estimated that more than 100,000 tires remained in Puget Sound from the old reef program, while noting that the exact number is uncertain because not all tire placements are mapped. DNR has identified multiple priority sites, and its work involves locating tire piles, recovering them from the water and sending the damaged material for appropriate disposal.The original reefs were intended to solve a fisheries problem by adding structure to the seabed, and decades later, the same structures have become objects that marine managers are trying to remove. The contrast has also shaped how newer artificial reefs in Puget Sound are designed, with greater attention to durable materials, site selection and long-term maintenance.
Article Summary: Discarded vehicle tires, among other materials, were bundled together and lowered into the water at 20 reef sites during the 1970s. The tires were tied together with polypropylene rope, and thousands were placed at each of the 20 sites. Washington's experiment with artificial reefs in Puget Sound began with the practical goal of creating more structure on the seafloor for rockfish, lingcod and other bottom-dwelling fish.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.

Article Title: Glance brings agentic shopping to iOS
Article Text:
FILE PHOTO: A customer compares his old iPhone with the newly launched iPhone 17 pro max at an Apple retail store in Delhi, India, September 19, 2025. REUTERS/Bhawika Chhabra/File Photo

Bengaluru:

InMobi’s lock-screen unicorn Glance has launched its agentic shopping experience natively on iOS, integrating with Siri AI to enable users to seek shopping assistance through voice commands, as the company looks to shift shopping from apps to AI agents. Glance has clocked around $300 million in revenue.The platform combines Apple Intelligence with Glance’s three-layered technology stack and understanding of users’ past preferences and context to explain why a product may be relevant to them. The experience uses Apple ’s Liquid Glass design language and adapts across iPhone and iPad.The integration follows a long collaboration between Glance and Apple across three areas — Apple Intelligence and Siri, Apple’s on-device models, and adaptive experiences across screens — according to InMobi founder and CEO Naveen Tewari.“Together, we worked on bringing agentic commerce directly into this experience, enabling a consumer’s shopping intent to translate into discovery and action,” Tewari said in a LinkedIn post.While Glance’s app has been available on the App Store, this is the company’s first direct integration into Apple’s core intelligence framework. It is an agent-to-agent integration with Siri rather than a lock-screen integration.Users upgrading to iOS 27 will be able to access Glance intelligence through Siri.For instance, users can photograph an apparel item and ask Siri where it can be bought. The Glance Agent can identify the product, surface relevant options and enable a virtual try-on experience.Glance has integrated Apple’s on-device models with its commerce intelligence. Its iOS experience uses Foundation Models and Core AI to enable on-device virtual try-ons, including image generation directly on the iPhone. The feature is currently experimental and is being developed with a focus on privacy.“This is a very deep-tech collaboration. Our investment is more on how we co-build this agentic commerce experience on Apple Intelligence,” said Mansi Jain, COO at Glance. The investment has primarily been in people and technology, with Glance’s technology team working closely with Apple’s developer team.Jain said the partnership was significant for Glance’s global positioning. “We are the only platform which is building from India for the world which is showcased at the Apple stage,” she said.Glance currently has 10 million monthly active users in the US and said around 15% of users are transacting through its agent. The company has not disclosed GMV.Glance expects more than 50.0% of consumers to shop through agents over the next two to three years. Jain said the Apple integration validates the company’s thesis that consumers will increasingly use agents for shopping.The company expects iOS users to have higher transaction values, with Jain saying industry ARPU (average revenue per user) for iOS users is typically about twice that of Android users.
Article Summary: InMobi’s lock-screen unicorn Glance has launched its agentic shopping experience natively on iOS. Users upgrading to iOS 27 will be able to access Glance intelligence through Siri. Glance expects more than 50.0% of consumers to shop through agents over the next two to three years.

The prices of 512GB iPhone 17 has risen by Rs 22,000, while 1TB iPhone Air costs Rs 65,000 more than before, an increase of 40.7%.These are increases on the devices themselves, rather than comparisons between successive Pro generations.The revised prices arrive as buyers prepare for festive shopping. For consumers comparing models, the distinction between official prices and the final purchase cost will matter. Retailer discounts, exchange benefits and payment offers will determine the eventual bill.
Article Summary: Apple has raised prices across its India line-up ahead of festive sales. The increases cover iPhone 16, iPhone 17e, iPhone Air and newly launched iPhone 18 Pro series. Traditionally, Apple slashes prices of previous generation iPhones when it launches a new model.

Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.
